name: The Council Oak
summary: The oldest tree in the park, older than the city. The first parks board met under it in 1889.
body: The oak was here when the land was a farm, and the farmer plowed around it. Its crown is 96 feet across. A lightning protection system was fitted in 1998.

name: Tanner's Sycamore
where: Tanner's Run, by the old tannery
summary: A white-barked giant leaning over the creek where the tannery stood.
body: The tannery closed in 1901; the sycamore seeded itself in its yard. Its bark peels in plates, leaving the upper limbs white.

name: The Pond Willow
summary: The willow on every postcard of the Wallow. Being monitored after a limb failure in 2025.
body: A large limb split in a summer storm in 2025. The city arborist cabled the two main leaders and checks it every quarter.

name: Hillcrest Beech
summary: A smooth-barked beech on the Ridge Trail, watched for beech leaf disease.
body: Please do not carve the bark: carvings let disease in, and they never heal.

name: The Garden Ginkgos
summary: A male and female pair planted when the garden opened. They drop their leaves within a day or two each November.
body: The female tree's seeds smell strongly in the fall; the crew rake them twice a week from late October.

name: The Lightning Tulip
summary: The tallest tree in the park, scarred by lightning in 1987 and still growing.
body: The scar runs 40 feet down the trunk. Woodpeckers nest in it every spring.

name: Elm Walk Survivors
summary: Three elms left from the avenue of 64 planted in 1898. The rest were lost to Dutch elm disease.
body: The three survivors are injected against the disease every three years. The new avenue trees are disease-resistant elms planted from 2012.

name: Outflow Bald Cypress
summary: A southern tree planted far from home, now with knees poking out of the shallows.
body: The knees are woody roots that rise above the water. Please keep off them: they bruise easily.
